i kinda wish dots was a standalone app and not part of chatgpt. 

as it stands, it feels like a product feature (e.g. GPTs) and not a big, exciting new release.

i might understand why they did it though - chatgpt is the canonical application-layer brand for openai, and creating a separate product would create contention with this brand. they had already spent a lot of work unifying codex, work, and chat into the desktop app. they have to support existing interaction patterns with chtgpt but also evolve into this new world of cloud agents and always-on assistants. 

any company willing to launch a new focused agent product (instinct / muse) will then have an advantage, because they will be able to concentrate mindshare around the specific space they are known for. openai could do it, but at the risk of cannibalizing the chatgpt brand. feels like some version of the innovators dilemma

Intent Advanced caught 93.0% of the bugs, the highest of any agent we tested, at 63% lower cost per review than the top baseline. It's built for high-stakes changes like database migrations, core infrastructure, and security policy edits.

For everyday changes, Intent Balanced caught 79.4%, close to Claude Code with Opus 5.0 at 81.3%, while cutting review cost by 95%. Most engineering work is routine updates, so review needs to stay affordable at that volume.

reviewedPosts.author: jiayq
reviewedPosts.text:
We started with about 10,000 bug-fix pull requests from real-world projects where the commit that introduced the bug was known. After auditing each one, we kept 284 tasks across 57 repositories and seven languages.

Each task mirrors a real code review. The agent sees the commit that introduced the bug, with full repository context, but never the fix. A judge agent counts it as caught only if it names the right root cause in the right place.

reviewedPosts.author: joaomdmoura
reviewedPosts.text:
A while ago I was trying to sell CrewAI to a huge bank.

They liked the platform. Then they asked how they would do observability, and I had to say they would need to buy something else.

Then memory. Same answer.

By the third answer they were sitting there thinking, alright, I have to buy five products to use yours.

That meeting ended an argument we had been having internally for months.

Everyone can tell you the stack is fragmenting. Data, models, orchestration, observability, connection, interface. Every layer pulling in companies who want to own exactly one thing.

Sit on the other side of the table and it flips.

Nobody wants five contracts. Five security reviews. Five vendors to chase at 2am. They want one number to call.

So what do you do when the market pulls apart and the buyer pulls together?

You build the boring parts anyway. Deployment, traces, PII, permissions, the governance a bank asks about first.

Architecture arguments get settled by procurement. Not by engineers.

reviewedPosts.text:
How many people show up on a Tuesday night to talk about document processing for AI agents? 🤔

In New York, enough to fill the room and start a waitlist. In San Francisco, almost 600.

We were in both cities on the same night to talk about one problem: agents don't read documents the way people do. Look at an invoice and you can tell the monthly rate from the total in a second. An agent often gets the words without the layout, so it has to guess.

In New York, we partnered with @usekernel on @braintrust's Agent Builders Night. In San Francisco, we partnered with @WorkOS on @daytonaio's AI Builders event. Thanks to them for having us, and to Abrar and Yong from our team for speaking!

Over the last 50 years, computer-aided design has revolutionised almost every major engineering field – but its revolution in making medicines has only just begun.

Moving from manual execution to AI-driven design unlocks a depth and scale that was previously impossible. Our drug design engine, IsoDDE, intelligently searches vast chemical spaces to design functional molecules ready for the real world. What used to take months of lab work now happens computationally in just days.

The visualisation below is a representation of our drug design agent working autonomously over a 2-4 day period. Starting with a strict design specification (the biological target and desired molecular properties), our AI agent autonomously searches and iteratively generates new molecule designs that result in real world functional progress.
